## 任务：检查 exp-006 是否全部完成，如完成则汇总结果并启动 exp-015

### 背景
exp-006 graduated filtering 实验在 westc-26893 上运行，共 51 runs（6 strategies × 5 seeds + 1 base_model）。上次检查 48/51 完成，剩余 dsir_s456（评估中）、dsir_s789、dsir_s1024。

### 步骤 1：检查 exp-006 完成状态

SSH 到 westc-26893，执行以下检查：

```bash
# 1. 检查训练进程
ps aux | grep -E "exp006|filtering|lm_eval" | grep -v grep

# 2. 检查 tmux session
tmux list-sessions 2>/dev/null

# 3. 检查结果文件数量
ls /root/autodl-tmp/gen-depth-contamination/artifacts/exp006_filtering/results/*.json 2>/dev/null | wc -l

# 4. 列出所有结果文件
ls -lt /root/autodl-tmp/gen-depth-contamination/artifacts/exp006_filtering/results/*.json 2>/dev/null

# 5. 特别检查 dsir 的 5 个 seed 结果
ls /root/autodl-tmp/gen-depth-contamination/artifacts/exp006_filtering/results/dsir_s*.json 2>/dev/null
```

### 步骤 2：如果全部 51 runs 完成

汇总所有 6 策略的结果。读取每个 JSON 结果文件，提取 MMLU 和 HellaSwag 指标。

```bash
# 读取所有结果，汇总为表格
cd /root/autodl-tmp/gen-depth-contamination/artifacts/exp006_filtering/results/
for f in *.json; do
    echo "=== $f ==="
    python3 -c "
import json
with open('$f') as fp:
    d = json.load(fp)
mmlu = d.get('mmlu', d.get('results', {}).get('mmlu', {}).get('acc', 'N/A'))
hs = d.get('hellaswag', d.get('results', {}).get('hellaswag', {}).get('acc_norm', 'N/A'))
print(f'MMLU: {mmlu}, HellaSwag: {hs}')
" 2>/dev/null || echo "Failed to parse"
done
```

如果 JSON 结构不同，先看一个文件的完整结构：
```bash
python3 -c "import json; print(json.dumps(json.load(open('no_filter_s42.json')), indent=2))" 2>/dev/null | head -30
```

**最终需要的输出格式**：
| Strategy | MMLU (mean±std) | HellaSwag (mean±std) |
按 MMLU 降序排列，包含所有 6 个策略 + base_model。

### 步骤 3：检查 GPU 状态
```bash
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv,noheader
```

### 步骤 4：如果 exp-006 完成且 GPU 空闲，启动 exp-015

exp-015 是 neural probe 重跑实验，脚本已修好 OOM 问题。Director 已预批准，无需等审批。

```bash
# 检查脚本存在
ls -la /root/autodl-tmp/gen-depth-contamination/scripts/run_exp015_neural_probe.py

# 在 tmux 中启动
tmux new-session -d -s exp015 'source /root/miniconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && conda activate base && cd /root/autodl-tmp/gen-depth-contamination && python3 scripts/run_exp015_neural_probe.py 2>&1 | tee logs/exp015_neural_probe_v3.log'

# 确认启动成功
sleep 5
tmux capture-pane -t exp015 -p | tail -20
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv,noheader
```

### 产出
1. exp-006 完成状态：X/51
2. 如完成：6 策略 + base_model 的 MMLU/HellaSwag 表格
3. GPU 状态
4. exp-015 是否已启动（如 exp-006 完成）

\section{Application: $\Kstar$-Aware Data Filtering}
\label{sec:filtering}

$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement beyond the binary boundary provides no additional benefit over binary filtering.
We compare six data curation strategies on a corpus of 30{,}000 documents (5{,}000 per depth, depths 0--5): (i)~\textbf{no-filter} (uniform weight), (ii)~\textbf{binary-ours} ($w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$ from the 15D LightGBM classifier), (iii)~\textbf{binary-Drayson} (importance weighting following \citet{drayson2025}, same classifier, weights $w_j \propto (1 - q(x_j))^b$, $b{=}1$, cap $r_{\max}{=}3$), (iv)~\textbf{graduated} (exponential decay $w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, $\alpha \in \{0.1,\ldots,0.9\}$), (v)~\textbf{surprisal} (retain documents above corpus median surprisal), and (vi)~\textbf{DSIR}~\citep{xie2023dsir} (importance resampling against depth-0 reference).

We fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA (rank~8, $\alpha_{\text{LoRA}}{=}16$) for 3 epochs, evaluating on MMLU (14{,}042 examples, 0-shot) and HellaSwag (10{,}042 examples, 0-shot) across 5 seeds; the graduated strategy is further crossed with 5~$\alpha$ values (51 total runs).

\paragraph{Results.}

% \input{tables/tab_filtering_main}  % DATA PENDING — re-enable after exp-006 data is filled

All strategies degrade absolute performance relative to the base model (MMLU 0.6018, HellaSwag 0.6821).
Binary-ours achieves the highest accuracy on both benchmarks (MMLU $0.5941 \pm 0.0009$; HellaSwag $0.6701 \pm 0.0006$), outperforming no-filter by $+$0.76\,pp / $+$0.63\,pp and binary-Drayson ($0.5913$; $0.6691$) by $+$0.28\,pp / $+$0.10\,pp.
Graduated filtering at its best $\alpha$ does not outperform binary-ours on either benchmark.
Surprisal-based selection (MMLU $0.5894 \pm 0.0010$; HellaSwag $0.6641 \pm 0.0006$) falls short by $-$0.47\,pp / $-$0.60\,pp.
DSIR results (\textbf{XX.XX}) are pending.

\paragraph{$\alpha$ sensitivity.}
Higher $\alpha$ values yield monotonically better performance on both benchmarks (HellaSwag: $0.6640$ at $\alpha{=}0.1$ to $0.6701$ at $\alpha{=}0.9$).
At $\alpha{=}0.9$, graduated filtering narrows the MMLU gap to 0.49\,pp below binary-ours ($0.5892$ vs.\ $0.5941$) and matches binary-ours exactly on HellaSwag ($0.6701$)---consistent with higher $\alpha$ progressively approximating binary thresholding.
The fact that even the best graduated configuration does not reach binary-ours confirms that ordinal depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ introduce noise rather than signal (detailed $\alpha$ sweep in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).

\paragraph{Summary.}
$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement provides no additional benefit.
Binary $\Kstar$-aware filtering is the most effective strategy among all tested approaches: neither ordinal depth weighting nor alternative quality signals (surprisal scoring) improve upon binary curation at the $\Kempirical$ boundary.

\section{Application: $\Kstar$-Aware Data Filtering}
\label{sec:filtering}

$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement beyond the binary boundary provides no additional benefit over binary filtering.
We compare six data curation strategies on a corpus of 30{,}000 documents (5{,}000 per depth, depths 0--5): (i)~\textbf{no-filter} (uniform weight), (ii)~\textbf{binary-ours} ($w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$ from the 15D LightGBM classifier), (iii)~\textbf{binary-Drayson} (importance weighting following \citet{drayson2025}, same classifier, weights $w_j \propto (1 - q(x_j))^b$, $b{=}1$, cap $r_{\max}{=}3$), (iv)~\textbf{graduated} (exponential decay $w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, $\alpha \in \{0.1,\ldots,0.9\}$), (v)~\textbf{surprisal} (retain documents above corpus median surprisal), and (vi)~\textbf{DSIR}~\citep{xie2023dsir} (importance resampling against depth-0 reference).

We fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA (rank~8, $\alpha_{\text{LoRA}}{=}16$) for 3 epochs, evaluating on MMLU (14{,}042 examples, 0-shot) and HellaSwag (10{,}042 examples, 0-shot) across 5 seeds; the graduated strategy is further crossed with 5~$\alpha$ values (51 total runs).

\paragraph{Results.}

% \input{tables/tab_filtering_main}  % DATA PENDING — re-enable after exp-006 data is filled

All strategies degrade absolute performance relative to the base model (MMLU 0.6018, HellaSwag 0.6821).
Binary-ours achieves the highest accuracy on both benchmarks (MMLU $0.5941 \pm 0.0009$; HellaSwag $0.6701 \pm 0.0006$), outperforming no-filter by $+$0.76\,pp / $+$0.63\,pp and binary-Drayson ($0.5913$; $0.6691$) by $+$0.28\,pp / $+$0.10\,pp.
Graduated filtering at its best $\alpha$ does not outperform binary-ours on either benchmark.
Surprisal-based selection (MMLU $0.5894 \pm 0.0010$; HellaSwag $0.6641 \pm 0.0006$) falls short by $-$0.47\,pp / $-$0.60\,pp.
DSIR performs worst among all strategies (MMLU $0.5869 \pm 0.0003$; HellaSwag $0.6631 \pm 0.0007$), only $+$0.04\,pp above no-filter on MMLU and $-$0.07\,pp below on HellaSwag---its bigram feature hashing captures domain shift but not the depth-correlated distributional signatures that our classifier exploits.

\paragraph{$\alpha$ sensitivity.}
Higher $\alpha$ values yield monotonically better performance on both benchmarks (HellaSwag: $0.6640$ at $\alpha{=}0.1$ to $0.6701$ at $\alpha{=}0.9$).
At $\alpha{=}0.9$, graduated filtering narrows the MMLU gap to 0.49\,pp below binary-ours ($0.5892$ vs.\ $0.5941$) and matches binary-ours exactly on HellaSwag ($0.6701$)---consistent with higher $\alpha$ progressively approximating binary thresholding.
The fact that even the best graduated configuration does not reach binary-ours confirms that ordinal depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ introduce noise rather than signal (detailed $\alpha$ sweep in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).

\paragraph{Summary.}
$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement provides no additional benefit.
Binary $\Kstar$-aware filtering is the most effective strategy among all tested approaches: neither ordinal depth weighting, surprisal scoring, nor distribution-matching (DSIR) improve upon binary curation at the $\Kempirical$ boundary.

\section{Application: $\Kstar$-Aware Data Filtering}
\label{sec:filtering}

$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement beyond the binary boundary provides no additional benefit over binary filtering.
We compare six data curation strategies on a corpus of 30{,}000 documents (5{,}000 per depth, depths 0--5): (i)~\textbf{no-filter} (uniform weight), (ii)~\textbf{binary-ours} ($w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$ from the 15D LightGBM classifier), (iii)~\textbf{binary-Drayson} (importance weighting following \citet{drayson2025}, same classifier, weights $w_j \propto (1 - q(x_j))^b$, $b{=}1$, cap $r_{\max}{=}3$), (iv)~\textbf{graduated} (exponential decay $w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, $\alpha \in \{0.1,\ldots,0.9\}$), (v)~\textbf{surprisal} (retain documents above corpus median surprisal), and (vi)~\textbf{DSIR}~\citep{xie2023dsir} (importance resampling against depth-0 reference).

We fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA (rank~8, $\alpha_{\text{LoRA}}{=}16$) for 3 epochs, evaluating on MMLU (14{,}042 examples, 0-shot) and HellaSwag (10{,}042 examples, 0-shot) across 5 seeds; the graduated strategy is further crossed with 5~$\alpha$ values (51 total runs).

\paragraph{Results.}

% \input{tables/tab_filtering_main}  % DATA PENDING — re-enable after exp-006 data is filled

All strategies degrade absolute performance relative to the base model (MMLU 0.6018, HellaSwag 0.6821).
Binary-ours achieves the highest accuracy on both benchmarks (MMLU $0.5941 \pm 0.0008$; HellaSwag $0.6701 \pm 0.0006$), outperforming no-filter by $+$0.76\,pp / $+$0.63\,pp and binary-Drayson ($0.5913$; $0.6691$) by $+$0.28\,pp / $+$0.10\,pp.
Graduated filtering at its best $\alpha$ does not outperform binary-ours on either benchmark.
Surprisal-based selection (MMLU $0.5894 \pm 0.0010$; HellaSwag $0.6641 \pm 0.0006$) falls short by $-$0.47\,pp / $-$0.60\,pp.
DSIR performs worst among all strategies (MMLU $0.5869 \pm 0.0003$; HellaSwag $0.6631 \pm 0.0007$), only $+$0.04\,pp above no-filter on MMLU and $-$0.07\,pp below on HellaSwag---its bigram feature hashing captures domain shift but not the depth-correlated distributional signatures that our classifier exploits.

\paragraph{$\alpha$ sensitivity.}
Higher $\alpha$ values yield monotonically better performance on both benchmarks (HellaSwag: $0.6640$ at $\alpha{=}0.1$ to $0.6701$ at $\alpha{=}0.9$).
At $\alpha{=}0.9$, graduated filtering narrows the MMLU gap to 0.49\,pp below binary-ours ($0.5892$ vs.\ $0.5941$) and matches binary-ours exactly on HellaSwag ($0.6701$)---consistent with higher $\alpha$ progressively approximating binary thresholding.
The fact that even the best graduated configuration does not reach binary-ours confirms that ordinal depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ introduce noise rather than signal (detailed $\alpha$ sweep in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).

\paragraph{Summary.}
$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement provides no additional benefit.
Binary $\Kstar$-aware filtering is the most effective strategy among all tested approaches: neither ordinal depth weighting, surprisal scoring, nor distribution-matching (DSIR) improve upon binary curation at the $\Kempirical$ boundary.

13	All strategies degrade absolute performance relative to the base model (MMLU 0.6018, HellaSwag 0.6821).
14	Binary-ours achieves the highest accuracy on both benchmarks (MMLU $0.5941 \pm 0.0008$; HellaSwag $0.6701 \pm 0.0006$), outperforming no-filter by $+$0.76\,pp / $+$0.63\,pp and binary-Drayson ($0.5913$; $0.6691$) by $+$0.28\,pp / $+$0.10\,pp.
15	Graduated filtering at its best $\alpha$ does not outperform binary-ours on either benchmark.
16	Surprisal-based selection (MMLU $0.5894 \pm 0.0009$; HellaSwag $0.6641 \pm 0.0006$) falls short by $-$0.47\,pp / $-$0.60\,pp.
17	DSIR performs worst among all strategies (MMLU $0.5869 \pm 0.0003$; HellaSwag $0.6631 \pm 0.0007$), only $+$0.04\,pp above no-filter on MMLU and $-$0.07\,pp below on HellaSwag---its bigram feature hashing captures domain shift but not the depth-correlated distributional signatures that our classifier exploits.
18	
19	\paragraph{$\alpha$ sensitivity.}
20	Higher $\alpha$ values yield monotonically better performance on both benchmarks (HellaSwag: $0.6640$ at $\alpha{=}0.1$ to $0.6701$ at $\alpha{=}0.9$).
21	At $\alpha{=}0.9$, graduated filtering narrows the MMLU gap to 0.49\,pp below binary-ours ($0.5892$ vs.\ $0.5941$) and matches binary-ours exactly on HellaSwag ($0.6701$)---consistent with higher $\alpha$ progressively approximating binary thresholding.
22	The fact that even the best graduated configuration does not reach binary-ours confirms that ordinal depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ introduce noise rather than signal (detailed $\alpha$ sweep in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
23	
24	\paragraph{Summary.}
25	$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement provides no additional benefit.
26	Binary $\Kstar$-aware filtering is the most effective strategy among all tested approaches: neither ordinal depth weighting, surprisal scoring, nor distribution-matching (DSIR) improve upon binary curation at the $\Kempirical$ boundary.
